title: Getting Oriented
answer: The first four chapters lay the foundation for everything that follows. They explain what AI can and cannot do, the ten patterns that account for nearly every idea in the Volume, the laws and rules that protect students, and a simple method for piloting and measuring any new tool.

children.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do
children.blurb: In the fall of 2023, nearly 1,000 students at a high school in Turkey took part in a simple test. During math review sessions, some students practiced with a plain AI chat tool, much like the free chatbots anyone can open on a phone.

children.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere
children.blurb: When this Volume began, the raw material was a stack of 1,200 ideas for using AI in schools, gathered from teachers, district leaders, researchers, and product lists. Reading them one by one felt like walking through a crowded market where every stall sold something slightly different.

children.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule
children.blurb: In June 2026, a school board member in Portland, Oregon, raised concerns about the data an AI reading assessment company would collect from students. The list of data fields in the company's contract included items such as place of birth and migrant status (Willamette Week, 2026).

children.name: Pilot, Measure, Scale
children.blurb: In a recent trial in Germany, 371 students in grades 7 through 9 used generative AI tools during six regular physics and English lessons. Some students got a tool designed to build motivation, some got a tool designed to teach learning strategies, and a comparison group used a plain chatbot.

sections.body: Getting Oriented is the opening part of the book's treatment of AI in education. It is made up of the first four chapters, which together lay the foundation for everything that follows. In this part, the book sets out what AI can and cannot do before any later idea is used. It also explains the ten patterns that account for nearly every idea in the Volume, the laws and rules that protect students, and a simple method for piloting and measuring any new tool. Readers who start nowhere else should start here.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that beginning with these four chapters works because they give readers the base they need for later ideas. It also holds that the rules set out in these chapters apply to every idea in the chapters that follow. The text does not name a practice that does not work in this section, but it does not treat later ideas as free from these rules. The rule it holds to is that orientation comes first and that the same foundation governs everything after it. This makes the section a starting point rather than an optional introduction.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The four pages fit together as the first four chapters of the foundation. What AI Can and Cannot Do gives the basic limits and abilities, while Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere gives the recurring ideas that appear across the Volume. Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule covers the laws and rules that protect students, and Pilot, Measure, Scale gives the simple method for trying and measuring any new tool. A teacher would go to What AI Can and Cannot Do and Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere to understand limits and recurring ideas, while a leader would go to Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule and Pilot, Measure, Scale for student protections and a method to pilot and measure tools. A parent would go to Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule to see the laws and rules that protect students.
